summary: San Bernardino sprawls across 62.5 square miles at the foot of the San Bernardino Mountains, and from certain vantage points you can look north straight up at peaks topping 10,000 feet — a dramatic backdrop that belies the city's position on the Inland Empire valley floor. That proximity to San Bernardino National Forest means genuine mountain trail access within a short drive, yet the city itself is largely flat and car-dependent, its grid fragmented by the I-215 and I-10 interchange cutting through the urban core. At a median home price of $384,900 against a median household income of roughly $64,000, the price-to-income ratio sits around 6:1 — more accessible than coastal Southern California but still a stretch without dual incomes, and the $1,433 median rent consumes over a quarter of that median gross pay. The local economy leans heavily on logistics, healthcare (several major hospital systems operate here), government, and education — including Cal State San Bernardino — so employment options exist without commuting west, though tens of thousands still make the I-10 slog toward Los Angeles or Orange County. With 9.6 hours of daily sunshine on average and daytime highs around 78°F year-round, summers push well past 100°F while winters stay mild, making this a place where air conditioning isn't optional but heating rarely matters. The property crime rate of 3,178 per 100,000 and violent crime rate above 1,000 per 100,000 are significantly elevated compared to national averages — a reality reflected in municipal budget debates and policing discussions that have persisted for years. San Bernardino is a city where mountain grandeur and valley affordability sit in direct tension with infrastructure strain and public-safety statistics that demand clear-eyed attention.
